To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) CT screening for lung cancer is safe; (2) CT screening for early lung cancer is effective in reducing lung cancer mortality; (3) CT screening for the early detection of lung cancer is feasible; and (4) CT screening for small lung cancer is cost-effective.
CT screening for early lung cancer detection has the potential to reduce lung cancer deaths in high-risk individuals.

1) CT screening reduces lung cancer mortality in high-risk populations; 2) the benefit of CT screening is greater in smokers than in former smokers; and 3) CT screening is not cost effective in high-risk populations, even if it reduces lung cancer mortality.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: What is the effect of CT screening on lung cancer mortality?
the use of a novel, low-cost, and noninvasive imaging technique to detect lung cancer in patients with no symptoms.
the development and application of mathematical and statistical methods in the analysis and modelling of data.

the current evidence does not support the routine screening of asymptomatic individuals with LDCT for lung cancer.
screening for lung cancer with CT is not yet recommended for the general population.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the CT screening is a safe procedure and that the benefits are greater than the risks.
the use of CT screening for lung cancer is associated with a reduction in lung cancer mortality of about 20%.
we have shown the feasibility of using CT screening for lung cancer detection and that we have shown a reduction in mortality from lung cancer in high-risk populations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have shown that a low-cost, low-dose, and low-radiation CT scan can be used to screen for lung cancer.
the current evidence is not strong enough to justify the use of CT screening for lung cancer in the general population.
